title: River red gum

names.gloss: water gum tree; this tree is good timber for woomeras (yalanji dialect)

identification.basis: The dictionary has three words for white or 'baldy' gums and two for a 'water gum tree' but does not say which smooth-barked gum each is. The river red gum is the smooth white gum of the Mitchell's banks, with 22 Atlas records within 30 km of Karma Waters, so one of these words is likely to be it; the match is not recorded.

summary: The big smooth-barked gum of the inland river banks is the **river red gum**, and the dictionary's words for the smooth gums are **[kayjurr](word:kayjurr)** 'white gum', **[bajar](word:bajar)** 'species of white gum', **[jabarr](word:jabarr)** 'baldy gum tree', and **[jinajina](word:jinajina)** (Nyungkul **[dakumbar](word:dakumbar)**) 'water gum tree; this tree is good timber for woomeras' [ref:hershberger1982]. It is 'a tree with smooth white or cream-coloured bark, lance-shaped or curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven or nine, white flowers and hemispherical fruit with the valves extending beyond the rim. A familiar and iconic tree, it is seen along many watercourses across inland Australia, providing shade in the extreme temperatures' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis]. '*Eucalyptus camaldulensis* has the widest natural distribution of any eucalyptus species. It is commonly found along waterways and there are only a few locations where the species is found away from a watercourse', which makes it the surest sign of water in dry country [ref:wiki-camaldulensis]. It is the river's shade, honey, hollows and firewood, and its one famous danger: 'the limbs of river red gums, sometimes whole trees, often fall without warning so that camping or picnicking near them is dangerous' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary classes the eucalypts by their bark, as the botanists do, and the smooth ones are the 'white' and 'baldy' gums: **[kayjurr](word:kayjurr)** 'white gum', **[bajar](word:bajar)** 'species of white gum', **[jabarr](word:jabarr)** 'baldy gum tree'. Its 'water gum tree' is **[jinajina](word:jinajina)** in Yalanji, 'this tree is good timber for woomeras', and **[dakumbar](word:dakumbar)** in Nyungkul [ref:hershberger1982]. On the coast where the dictionary was made there are several smooth gums and a water gum, so which word belongs to the river red gum of the inland rivers is not recorded; the [woodland](entry:woodland) page puts *kayjurr* and *jabarr* with the gums as a class. **[nyumbil](word:nyumbil)** 'coolibah tree (messmate)' is the dictionary's word for the other flood-country gum, and **[wankar](word:wankar)**, 'a tree which grows along the water and has red flowers', fits the weeping bottlebrush of the same banks [ref:hershberger1982]. The river red gum's Northern Territory Aboriginal names are listed on its Wikipedia page [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
'*Eucalyptus camaldulensis* is a tree that typically grows to a height of 20 metres but sometimes to 45 metres and often does not develop a lignotuber. The bark is smooth white or cream-coloured with patches of yellow, pink or brown. There are often loose, rough slabs of bark near the base. The juvenile leaves are lance-shaped, 80–180 mm long and 13–25 mm wide. Adult leaves are lance-shaped to curved, the same dull green or greyish green colour on both sides, 50–300 mm long and 7–32 mm wide'. 'The flower buds are arranged in groups of seven, nine or sometimes eleven', 'with a prominently beaked operculum'. 'Flowering mainly occurs in summer and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, hemispherical capsule 2–5 mm long and 4–10 mm wide ... with the valves raised above the rim.' 'The plant's flowers bloom for a long time throughout the year' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

**Water and flood.** 'The species can be found along the banks of watercourses, as well as the floodplains of those watercourses. Due to the proximity to these watercourses, river red gum is subject to regular flooding in its natural habitat. River red gum prefers soils with clay content. The trees not only rely on rainfall but also on regular flooding, since flooding recharges the sub-soil with water.' 'The dry river beds of central Australia have sufficient underground water flow to sustain the trees' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

**What it gives the river.** 'The association of the river red gum with water makes the tree a natural habitat choice, indeed sometimes the only choice in drier areas, for other species. The trees provide a breeding habitat for fish during the flooding season, which also benefits aquatic bird life that depend on fish as a food source during their own breeding season.' 'River red gums contribute to the provision of nutrients and energy for other species through leaf and insect fall. This is especially important to the ecology in areas of low nutrients. The tree's preferred habitat of floodplains and watercourses also gives it the role of flood mitigator, which slows silt runoff' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

**Kino.** The dark red gum that bleeds from a wound in the bark is a kino, and 'Australian, Botany Bay, or Eucalyptus kino from *Eucalyptus siderophloia* and *Eucalyptus camaldulensis*, were imported into the United States' as a drug; 'the drug was frequently used in diarrhoea' and as a gargle, until better medicines replaced it [ref:wiki-kino]. See [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) and [bush medicine](entry:bush-medicine).

sections.heading: Telling it from the other gums
sections.body:
- **River red gum**: smooth white bark with coloured patches, rough slabs only at the butt, on the river bank; small fruit with the valves sticking out [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Dallachy's gum** and the other smooth gums of the hills: on the ridges, not the bank; see [woodland](entry:woodland).
- **Carbeen / Moreton Bay ash** (*bajar* in the woodland page's reading): tessellated bark on the bottom metres, then abruptly smooth [ref:hershberger1982].
- **[Paperbark](entry:paperbark)**: papery layers, bottlebrush flowers.
- **[Leichhardt tree](entry:leichhardt-tree)**: big glossy leaves, round fruit, bare in the dry.
- **[Ironbark](entry:woodland)** and **[bloodwood](entry:bloodwood)**: rough bark the whole way up.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A line of white gums across dry country** is a creek, and water under the sand [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Blossom in summer** roaring with bees by day and [flying foxes](entry:flying-foxes-and-bats) by night [ref:wiki-camaldulensis] [ref:wiki-lrff].
- **Hollows with a parrot's head in them**, and the cockatoos' chewed entrances; see [cockatoos and parrots](entry:cockatoos-and-parrots).
- **Red kino** running from a wound [ref:wiki-kino].
- **Fresh-dropped limbs** on the sand under a tree: the tree's warning [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Flood debris** lodged in the forks shows the last wet's height.

sections.heading: Where it grows
sections.body: The bank and floodplain of rivers and creeks, over bare sand and leaf litter: 'there are only a few locations where the species is found away from a watercourse' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

sections.heading: The river's tree
sections.body: Everything in the [waterhole](entry:waterhole) runs partly on the red gum: its leaf and insect fall feed the pool's bottom, its flood-time roots are 'a breeding habitat for fish', its shade keeps the pool cool, its blossom feeds the [native bees](entry:native-bees), the lorikeets and the flying foxes, its hollows house the [possums](entry:possums), the [parrots](entry:cockatoos-and-parrots), the [ducks](entry:ducks-and-geese) and the [kookaburras](entry:kookaburras-and-kingfishers), and its fallen limbs are the snags the [barramundi](entry:barramundi) and [sleepy cod](entry:sleepy-cod) lie under [ref:wiki-camaldulensis] [ref:wiki-lrff] [ref:wiki-brushtail]. The rosellas eat its seed [ref:wiki-rosella]. It needs the flood as much as the fish do: 'infrequent flooding ... provides inadequate water to recharge the floodplain subsoils that river red gums depend on. This will result in stunted tree growth, death of existing trees' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Flowers 'mainly ... in summer' and on and off through the year; seed shed 'mostly in spring and summer', some 'carried by the wind and water'; the flood in the wet recharges the ground it lives on [ref:wiki-camaldulensis]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Finding water**: the tree is the sign; see [finding water](entry:finding-water) [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Shade** for the camp, with the limb warning below [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Woomera timber**, if the dictionary's water gum is this tree: 'this tree is good timber for woomeras' [ref:hershberger1982]. See [spear and woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera).
- **Honey**: a summer blossom tree for the [sugarbag](entry:native-bees) [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Kino** as a gum and, historically, a medicine [ref:wiki-kino].
- **Firewood**: dense, slow, hot coals; the [earth oven's](entry:earth-oven) wood on the river.

sections.heading: Camping under red gums
sections.body:
1. **Look up before you camp**: dead limbs, a split fork, a hollow trunk, a tree stressed by drought; 'the limbs of river red gums, sometimes whole trees, often fall without warning' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
2. **Camp outside the drip line** of the biggest trees, in the open or under the paperbarks, and never in a wind.
3. **Take firewood from the ground**, not the tree; the dropped limbs are already seasoned.
4. **Follow the gums to water** across dry country: where the line of white trunks goes, the creek goes, and a soak is under the sand at the bend; see [finding water](entry:finding-water) [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
5. **Leave the hollow trees**; they are the river's nests.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Falling limbs: 'camping or picnicking near them is dangerous, especially if a tree has dead limbs or the tree is under stress' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- The pool under it is the crocodile's; see [Crocwise](entry:freshwater-crocodile) [ref:crocwise].
- Kino was a medicine once; it is a strong astringent and not a thing to eat from the tree [ref:wiki-kino].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Each place below says whose country the red gums stand on and where to camp. Which of the dictionary's gum words is this tree is for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: River red gums stand along the big streams of the Hann country. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 46 river red gum records, from 1973 to 2010, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann], and the Queensland Herbarium's paperbark fringe of this country's major streams carries '*Eucalyptus tereticornis* (blue gum) or *E. camaldulensis* (river red gum)' over the silver-crowned paperbarks [ref:qld-re]. The Kuku Thaypan Elders know the gums of the lagoons, river banks and plains as **Ku garl**, gum tree country, with its own time to burn [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Names here
sections.body: In Kuku Thaypan, *ku* begins the name of every tree [ref:standley2019]. **Ku garl** (also written *Ku agawl* and *Ku awgarl*) is 'Gum Tree', *Eucalyptus* sp., and Standley names the gums of Ku garl country as *E. tereticornis* and *E. tessellaris* [ref:standley2019]. Whether the Elders count the river red gum among them, the thesis does not say. The Kuku Yalanji words above are not this country's.

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body:
Ku garl country is 'around lagoon systems, riverine woodland and open eucalypt grassy woodlands on plains. Water settles in these systems from the wet season and they have hard brown dark soil'. The Elders group its gum communities 'according to where this system occurs in the landscape, for example on open plains, surrounding lagoons or on river banks' [ref:standley2019].

The Herbarium's river fringe (regional ecosystem 3.3.10a) is the river-bank kind: paperbarks with blue gum or river red gum, a sub-canopy that often holds the cluster [fig](entry:fig), and a ground layer 'generally very sparse and regularly swept clear by floods' [ref:qld-re].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body:
The Hann floods in the wet, highest in February–March, and runs very low but never stops in September–November [ref:bom-105001b]; the river red gum depends on just such flooding to recharge the ground it lives on [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

In the Elders' fire calendar, 'Ku agawl Gum flowering' is one of the signs for the early-dry burns [ref:standley2019]. Gum country 'is ready for burning when the Ku akalmba Messmate is flowering. By this time of the year the gum tree communities have flowered and produced fruit. Gum tree community is one of the first systems to burn, the darker the soil the earlier the burn, lighter soils are burnt later.' The weather sign is 'the last of the light squally showers and the SE knock em down rain', 'when Eriachne sp is setting seed and bark has shed'. Gum country left unburnt for years needs a hotter fire than it otherwise would [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: What it gives here
sections.body: The Elders list Ku garl among the trees important for the native sugarbag bees [ref:standley2019], and sugarbag is **Arear** in Kuku Thaypan [ref:standley2019]. See [native bees](entry:native-bees). Nothing else is published on how the people of the Hann used the river red gum; for the rest, see *Uses* above.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, under native title determinations of November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Downstream, Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Native title holders may take timber and other resources for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs without the licences others need [ref:nta1993]; anyone else should ask before cutting. Camp clear of big gums: their limbs fall without warning [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].

locations.summary: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) it is the sixth most-recorded plant within 30 km, with twenty-two records, and the Queensland Herbarium maps it with the [Leichhardt tree](entry:leichhardt-tree) and the [paperbarks](entry:paperbark) in the fringing woodland of the river's channels and levees [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:re9314].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: On the Mitchell and its creeks it grows in the Herbarium's 'Melaleuca fringing woodland on channels and levees' with the [Leichhardt tree](entry:leichhardt-tree) [ref:re9314].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The red gums are the Karma Waters river camps' shade and their hazard; the campground rules and the induction say where to camp [ref:kw-camping] [ref:re9314].
